title: What staff training does the Life Insurance Code of Practice require?
description: Training commitments in the Life Insurance Code of Practice 2025 for sales, underwriting, claims and vulnerability roles, and what the 2026 review changes.
shortAnswer: The Life Insurance Code of Practice 2025, owned by the Council of Australian Life Insurers (CALI) and effective from March 1, 2025, commits subscribing insurers to ongoing role appropriate training for sales staff, technical competency before underwriters and claims assessors make decisions, role appropriate training to support vulnerable customers, and cultural awareness training for staff serving remote Indigenous communities. The Life Code Compliance Committee monitors compliance, and a redrafted Code is being prepared after a 2026 independent review.
keyTakeaways: The current Life Code took effect on March 1, 2025 and binds the insurers and reinsurers listed as subscribers on CALI's website. It is now published by CALI; the Financial Services Council's website no longer hosts it.
Clauses 2.18 and 2.19 require ongoing role appropriate sales training, plus extra training to correct shortcomings, covering five set topics.
Clauses 4.18 and 5.45 bar underwriters and claims assessors from making decisions until they have shown technical competency and an understanding of relevant laws, the Life Code and CALI standards.
Clauses 6.7, 6.15 and 6.16 add training on interpreters, customers experiencing vulnerability, and cultural awareness for remote Indigenous communities.
An independent review led by Peter Kell made 85 recommendations. CALI published its response on September 30, 2026, with complex workstreams due to conclude in the first half of 2027.
regulator: Life Code Compliance Committee (Life CCC); Code owned by the Council of Australian Life Insurers (CALI)
appliesTo: Life insurers and reinsurers that subscribe to the Life Code, listed on CALI's website
Staff of subscribers and their Authorised representatives when acting for the insurer
Independent Service Providers under service agreements made or renewed after the insurer is bound
Sales, underwriting, claims, complaints and customer support roles

sections.heading: What is the Life Insurance Code of Practice and who is bound by it?

blocks.text: The Life Insurance Code of Practice (the Life Code) is an industry code that sets enforceable standards for life insurers above the legal minimum. CALI's [Life Code page](https://cali.org.au/life-code/) says the current version "is effective from 1 March 2025" and covers product design, sales, communication timeframes, claims and complaints. Earlier versions applied from implementation to June 30, 2023 (version 1.0), July 1 to September 28, 2023 (version 2.0), followed by further editions that CALI lists on the same page.

Clause 1.13 of the [Life Insurance Code of Practice 2025](https://cali.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/CALI-003-LICOP-Life-Code-2025-v4-WEB_01.pdf) says the Code binds CALI members that are registered life insurance companies issuing life insurance policies, other CALI members authorized to issue them, and any other entity that formally agrees with CALI and the Life CCC to adopt it. Clause 1.10 says it does not apply to superannuation fund trustees, financial advice firms or advisers unless they adopt it. Clause 1.7 lists covered products, including term life, TPD, trauma, income protection, funeral insurance and consumer credit insurance issued by a life insurer.

Clause 1.15 is the anchor for training: insurers "will ensure our staff and Authorised representatives comply with" the Code when acting for the insurer. Clause 8.12 makes the consequence explicit: an insurer is in breach if its staff or Authorised representatives do not comply. The Code's guiding principles also commit insurers to build an ethical culture "supported by sound corporate governance practices and effective staff training".

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects the Life Insurance Code of Practice 2025 and CALI's published review response as at November 2026. The Code is being redrafted, so clause numbers and training commitments may change. Check CALI's Life Code page before relying on any clause.

sections.heading: What training does the Life Code require for sales staff?

blocks.text: Clause 2.18 commits insurers to give their own staff, and the staff of Authorised representatives who sell their policies, "ongoing role-appropriate training, as well as extra training to correct any shortcomings we find". Clause 2.19 says the training will cover five topics:

items: the insurer's Life Insurance Policies and the characteristics of customers in the target audience
the legal duties owed to customers when staff provide personal advice

blocks.text: Related clauses shape how sales training is governed. Clause 2.16 requires insurers to agree with Authorised representatives on their sales approach, staff training requirements and monitoring framework. Clause 2.20 requires compliance performance measures in sales incentive programs, with consequences for unacceptable practices such as pressure selling. Clause 2.24 says that where an unacceptable sales practice is found, the insurer will correct it "including with further education and training where appropriate". The target audience topic ties to the [design and distribution obligations](/regulations/design-and-distribution-obligations-staff-training).

sections.heading: What competency must underwriters and claims assessors show?

blocks.text: Underwriters and claims assessors must demonstrate competence before they make decisions, not merely complete a course. Clause 4.18 says insurers will ensure underwriters have appropriate skills and training, "including for Mental Health Conditions where applicable", and that they "will not make decisions for us until they have shown technical competency and an understanding of relevant laws (including anti-discrimination laws), Life Code requirements and CALI standards and guidance".

Clause 5.45 applies the same gate to claims assessors, who must have the skills and training (including for mental health where applicable) to make objective decisions and may not decide claims until they have shown technical competency and an understanding of all relevant laws, Life Code requirements and CALI standards and guidance. Clause 5.46 requires claims assessors' remuneration, including bonuses, to be consistent with the Code's principles.

Claims interviews carry their own commitments. Clause 5.27 requires an interviewer the insurer is satisfied has the appropriate training and experience to discuss a claim involving a mental health condition, where relevant, and clause 5.32 limits interviews to 90 minutes unless the customer agrees in writing to an extension. A competency gate of this kind is a form of [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency), and the method is set out in the guide to [setting up verification of competency](/guides/how-to-set-up-verification-of-competency).

sections.heading: What training does the Code require for customers experiencing vulnerability?

blocks.text: The Code requires role appropriate training so staff can recognize and respond to vulnerability. Clause 6.1 lists causes of vulnerability including age, disability, mental health conditions, language and literacy barriers, remote location, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander status, family violence, suicidality and financial distress.

items: **Clause 6.15:** internal policies and role appropriate training to help staff identify and understand vulnerability, consider each customer's needs, decide how to help them engage, and engage with empathy, compassion and respect.
**Clause 6.7:** relevant training for staff likely to be involved in communications requiring an interpreter.
**Clause 6.16:** cultural awareness training for staff who regularly help customers in remote Indigenous communities.
**Clause 6.3:** additional care with Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander customers buying funeral or other life insurance, because of the practice known as gratuitous concurrence.

sections.heading: How is the Code enforced, and what complaint timeframes must staff know?

blocks.text: The Life CCC monitors and enforces the Code and can sanction insurers for significant breaches. Under clause 8.11 insurers report to the Life CCC yearly about compliance and maintain a governance process to report to their board or executive management. Clause 8.13 requires a significant breach to be reported to the Life CCC within 30 business days of discovery, unless already reported to a regulator. Clause 8.21 lists sanctions including a formal warning, a compliance audit, corrective advertising and a community benefit payment of up to $100,000 to a charity.

Complaints staff need the Code's timeframes alongside ASIC's. Clause 7.13 commits to a final written response within 30 calendar days, and clause 7.17 sets 45 calendar days where a superannuation trustee owns the policy, consistent with the maximum timeframes in ASIC's [RG 271](https://download.asic.gov.au/media/3olo5aq5/rg271-published-2-september-2021.pdf). Clause 7.10 limits closing a complaint within 5 business days to cases resolved to the customer's satisfaction or explained. The [RG 271 complaints training page](/regulations/asic-rg-271-complaints-handling-training) covers the ASIC side.

sections.heading: What will change after the 2026 Life Code review?

blocks.text: A redrafted Life Code is coming, but as at November 2026 the 2025 Code remains the version in force. CALI's [response page](https://cali.org.au/life-code-response/) says the independent review began in October 2025. CALI welcomed the final report from reviewer Peter Kell, with 85 recommendations, on June 30, 2026, and published its [action plan](https://cali.org.au/life-insurers-outline-action-plan-for-a-stronger-life-code/) on September 30, 2026.

The action plan says the industry supports the majority of recommendations, with further work on more complex recommendations to conclude in the first half of 2027. Commitments relevant to training include access to "a real person with the right knowledge" during a claim, embedding mental health commitments into the main body of the Code, stronger family and domestic violence protections, and broader powers for the Life CCC. CALI has set up workstreams on mental health, claims handling, First Nations and funeral insurance. Training teams should plan a content review once the redrafted Code is published, using the approach in [how to update training when regulations change](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry represents the Life Code's clauses, roles and competency gates as a structured framework, so each underwriter, claims assessor or salesperson is linked to the concepts and assessment points they must demonstrate before acting. When the redrafted Code is published, the changed clauses identify which roles and assessments need revision, and each record shows the Code version it was assessed against.

faqs.q: Is the Life Insurance Code of Practice still an FSC code?
faqs.a: The current Code is published by the Council of Australian Life Insurers, whose website hosts the 2025 Code and all previous versions back to version 1.0. The Financial Services Council's website no longer has a life insurance policy area, so people searching for the FSC Life Code should use CALI's Life Code page.

faqs.q: Does the Life Code set a minimum number of training hours?
faqs.a: No. The Code sets topics and competency gates rather than hours. Sales training must be ongoing and role appropriate under clause 2.18, and underwriters and claims assessors must show technical competency before making decisions under clauses 4.18 and 5.45. Insurers decide the format, frequency and assessment method.

faqs.q: Does the Life Code apply to superannuation trustees and financial advisers?
faqs.a: Not unless they adopt it. Clause 1.10 says the Code does not apply to superannuation fund trustees, financial advice companies or financial advisers, or other industry participants unless they have adopted it. Insurers remain responsible for their own staff and Authorised representatives under clause 1.15.

faqs.q: Do outsourced claims and underwriting providers have to meet the Code?
faqs.a: Yes, for agreements entered or renewed after the insurer became bound. Clause 1.18 requires those service agreements to meet the relevant Code standards, and clause 1.22 limits contracts to providers who reasonably satisfy the insurer of their expertise, experience, qualifications and integrity.
